title: Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8:26–40)
hook: how can I understand unless someone shows me

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven chosen so the widows wouldn't be forgotten, the first deacons in Catholic tradition. Your line was serve the tables.

A desert road, south out of Jerusalem toward Gaza, in the heat of the day. A chariot is rolling home. In it sits a powerful man, the treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, a court official the text calls a eunuch. He has traveled a very long way to worship in Jerusalem. Now he's going home with a scroll in his lap, reading aloud, the way people often read then. And he's stuck: he can make out every word and still can't tell what it means.
screen: `A DESERT ROAD TO GAZA.` → `A TREASURER WITH A SCROLL.` → `EVERY WORD, AND NO MEANING.`

segments.voice: An angel sends Philip, one of the seven, to that empty road. The Spirit tells him: go near, join that chariot. So Philip runs alongside, hears the man reading the prophet Isaiah, and asks a plain question: do you understand what you're reading? The answer, in the Douay-Rheims, is disarmingly plain: "And how can I, unless some man shew me?" Then he invites Philip up to sit with him. Notice who is asking: a court official who can read, who owns a scroll, who traveled a very long way to pray. He isn't embarrassed to say, I need someone. And Philip doesn't lecture from the road. He climbs in and sits beside him. The passage is Isaiah's servant, led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent before his shearer. Is the prophet talking about himself, the man asks, or someone else? Beginning from that very scripture, Philip tells him about Jesus. Then they pass water, and the man says, "See, here is water: what doth hinder me from being baptized?" Nothing does. The chariot stops, both go down into the water, and Philip baptizes him. Then Philip is gone, and the man "went on his way rejoicing." Where was he from? The Greek says Ethiopia, which then meant the kingdom of Kush, up the Nile, south of Egypt. Ethiopian Christians today love this man as one of their own first believers. Catholics see the Church's way of teaching here: scripture, a guide who sits beside you, and then the sacrament.
screen: `DO YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU READ?` · `HOW CAN I, UNLESS SOME MAN SHOW ME?` · `PHILIP CLIMBS IN AND SITS DOWN.` · `HERE IS WATER.` · then, large: `HE WENT ON HIS WAY REJOICING.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who asked you something lately, a coworker stuck on a task, a kid with homework, a parent with a new phone, and picture doing what Philip did: not answering from the road, but climbing in and sitting beside them, starting from where they are. Then notice the thing you don't understand yet, and who you might ask. If you pray, ask for the patience of someone who runs alongside a chariot.
Ethiopian. The court official from the kingdom of Kush, honest enough to say he needed help understanding scripture, baptized by Philip on a desert road. Today's word.
Your line: how can I, unless. Even a treasurer with his own scroll needed someone beside him. Five hundred forty-two days now.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught the faith through catechesis: in parishes, adults preparing for baptism walk with a sponsor and catechists through the scriptures before receiving the sacraments, often at the Easter Vigil.

original.note: Greek: Ethiopian. the word the text uses for the man from Kush, far up the Nile.

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary meets a foreigner and converts him.
what it means: a powerful, learned man admits he needs a guide, and a deacon climbs in and sits beside him before he says a word about Jesus.

what a scholar hears: Ethiopia in the Greek meant Kush, on the upper Nile, and Candace was a royal title there, not a personal name. Luke places a man from the far south of the known world among the first baptized.

chat.says: Why did that official on the desert road need Philip? Couldn't he read the scroll himself?
options: He could read every word, but asked: how can I understand unless someone shows me?
He couldn't read at all, so Philip read the words of Isaiah aloud for him.
He had no scroll of his own, so Philip brought one and read it with him.
chat.meaning: The official could read and owned a scroll, but honestly asked for a guide. Philip sat beside him and explained, starting from Isaiah.

Gaza.meaning: a city south of Jerusalem; the desert road ran toward it

eunuch.meaning: the text's word for this court official

Isaiah.meaning: the prophet the man was reading

Kush.meaning: an ancient kingdom up the Nile, south of Egypt

notes: Confirm the Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Acts 8:31, 8:36 and 8:39 exactly.
The text identifies this Philip as the evangelist (one of the seven, Acts 6:5; 21:8), not Philip the apostle; confirm the framing.
Ethiopia = Kush/Meroë and Candace as a royal title follow standard commentaries; confirm.
'Ethiopian Christians love this man as one of their first believers': Ethiopian Orthodox tradition; confirm wording.
Acts 8:37 (the confession) is absent from many Greek manuscripts but present in the Vulgate and Douay; the script doesn't quote it.

Reviewer softened 'the way everyone read then' to 'the way people often read then' (how common silent reading was in antiquity is debated) and 'traveled for weeks' to 'a very long way' (journey length not given in the text).
